summary: Proposes conventions for writing X.500 Directory names in a form people find friendly, so users do not have to type long formal names. It builds on the OSI Directory and is an experimental proposal, not a standard. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 1781, RFC 3494.

eli5.summary: Imagine mailing a friend and writing just their name and town instead of a long formal address with every box filled in. This memo suggests ways to look people up with simple, friendly names.

questions: how to represent x.500 names for people
what is a user friendly name
how does x.500 user friendly naming work
what is a purported name in a directory
subtitle: An experiment in letting people look up X.500 directory entries by typing a short, guessable name instead of a full formal one.

tldr.problem: Plain use of the OSI Directory is not user friendly: it lacks a user-oriented notation and names are hard to guess.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines User Friendly Names (UFNs), which are purported names that drop attribute types and levels or use alternate values, and a default algorithm that matches them against the directory in the context of a local environment.
tldr.outcome: It was an Experimental protocol, not a standard, and it is now Historic, replaced by RFC 1781 and RFC 3494.

today: RFC 1484 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 1781 and RFC 3494, and it was only ever an Experimental proposal, not an Internet standard.

sections.title: Why User Friendly Naming
sections.content:
The OSI Directory aims at user friendly naming, but simple use does not deliver two things: a user-oriented notation and guessability. The memo wants a name to be typed in directly, with no form filling or complex dialogue, for example a name taken from a business card or an email message.

It builds on the string notation of RFC 1485 and relaxes some of its constraints. The result cannot be mapped to a distinguished name without a directory. It targets names that follow an organisationally oriented directory tree, and the author admits it may suit some applications poorly.
sections.eli5: You should be able to just type the name you heard at a meeting, not fill in a long form.

sections.title: User Friendly Names and Purported Names
sections.content:
A purported name is what a user types for resolution into one or more distinguished names. A User Friendly Name (UFN) is a purported name that is expected to resolve unambiguously. An example is Steve Hardcastle-Kille, Computer Science, University College London, GB. The memo advises that systems store names as distinguished names and use purported names only for input and display.

A purported name may differ from a distinguished name in several ways:

  • Type omission, using a default schema Common Name, (((Organisational Unit)*, Organisation,) Country), with rules for deriving the omitted types.
  • Abbreviation (leaving out the higher components) and component omission (leaving out an intermediate level).
  • Approximation, such as CS and UCL, and friendly country names such as UK or France instead of the two-letter code.
  • Local type keywords, so that "Organisation" can stand for O.
sections.eli5: A purported name is your best guess at someone's address. You can skip parts, shorten words, or spell it roughly, and the computer tries to figure out who you mean.

sections.title: Communicating Directory Names
sections.content:
Two forms can be exchanged between people: the Distinguished Name (DN) in the format of RFC 1485, and the UFN. The memo makes no recommendation between them, but lists merits. A DN is an unambiguous and stable reference and is used efficiently by the directory. A UFN can omit redundant type information, use alternate values that mean something to the recipient, and skip levels of the hierarchy.

When a UFN is communicated, it should be a form that resolves efficiently and unambiguously. Writing one is compared to writing a postal address: there are many legal ways, so care is needed to keep it unambiguous. The term "Directory Name" or "X.500 Name" covers either form.
sections.eli5: You can give someone the full official address, which is always exact, or a short nickname-style address, which is easier but needs care so it does not match two people.

sections.title: Matching a Purported Name
sections.content:
The memo gives a default algorithm and says it may be modified. Matching happens in a local environment: an ordered list of non-leaf directory entries that act as acceptable abbreviations, which depends on how many components were typed and should be controllable by the user. Components are matched one at a time. If a component resolves to a single name, matching continues as though the full name had been given.

A match is exact, good (unambiguous and exactly matching an attribute value) or poor (any other substring or approximate match). The suggested heuristics are: always follow an exact match; follow all good matches if there are no exact ones; prompt the user if there are only poor matches; and move to the next environment element if nothing matches.

The search depends on the level in the tree. At the top level, a two-character component is treated as a country code or an exact friendly name. Intermediate levels search for organisations, localities and organisational units with substring and approximate matches. At the bottom level, a leaf such as a person is matched against Common Name, Surname and User ID.
sections.eli5: The computer starts from a sensible spot, like your own department, and checks each word you typed against nearby names. If it is sure, it goes ahead. If it is only half sure, it asks you.

sections.title: Experience, Related Work and Open Issues
sections.content:
An experimental implementation by Colin Robbins was deployed within the "FRED" interface of the PSI Pilot and in a prototype interface for managing distribution lists. The memo reports that user reaction was favourable. Problems found: the algorithm works badly when a user guesses an organisational unit that is not directly below the organisation, and leading wildcards in substring searches may be inefficient, so only trailing wildcards might be preferable.

The memo compares four kinds of names (typed or untyped, ordered or unordered) and chooses untyped and ordered, with optional typing. It lists issues to resolve before an Internet Standard: potential ambiguity, whether the specification is actually used, performance, and the algorithm. The syntax is expected to be stable, but the resolving algorithm may change with experience. The memo says security issues are not discussed.
sections.eli5: People who tried it liked it, but it sometimes got confused when they guessed the wrong middle step, so the authors asked others to test and improve the idea.
